sections_before_months.heading: OVERVIEW
paragraphs: This plan covers 8 weeks of strategic content (2 pieces per month = 4 total in the quarter).

Each month explores a different thematic axis, but keeps one throughline: early-stage founders don't fail at finance because of bad spreadsheets, they fail because they treat cash like a scoreboard instead of a decision tool.

sections_before_months.heading: AUDIENCE
paragraphs: Pre-seed to Series A founders who just took on their first real finance responsibility and don't yet have a CFO.

sections_before_months.heading: STRUCTURE
bullets: January: Cash as a decision tool
February: The illusion of growth metrics

months.label: JANUARY / 2027
months.axis_title: THEMATIC AXIS: Cash as a Decision Tool
months.axis_description: What separates founders who use runway to make decisions from founders who just watch it shrink.

pautas.title: "Your runway number is real. Your runway feeling is not."

direcionamento.label: Common narrative
direcionamento.text: "We have 14 months of runway, we're fine"

direcionamento.label: Reality
direcionamento.text: Founders quietly extend their mental runway by ignoring hiring plans already agreed to, or planned spend increases

direcionamento.label: Angle
direcionamento.text: The number on the dashboard and the number a founder acts on are usually two different numbers

direcionamento.label: Thesis
direcionamento.text: "If your runway number hasn't changed your last three decisions, you don't have a runway number, you have a runway feeling."

pautas.central_question: Why do founders with 12 months of runway make the same decisions as founders with 3?
structure: Open with the gap between stated runway and behavior
Explain the hidden assumptions that inflate a runway number
Example: a founder who kept the runway number flat by not updating for a signed lease
Show a simple test to know if your runway number is decision-grade
Close with a checklist for making runway operational, not decorative
pautas.keywords: runway, cash management, startup finance, decision making
pautas.tone: Direct. Calls out the gap between saying and doing.

pautas.title: "Burn multiple is a report card. It should be a steering wheel."

direcionamento.label: Common narrative
direcionamento.text: "Investors want to see our burn multiple, so we track it"

direcionamento.label: Reality
direcionamento.text: Most founders check burn multiple after the quarter closes, when it's too late to change anything

direcionamento.label: Angle
direcionamento.text: A metric only earns its keep if it changes a decision before the period ends, not after

direcionamento.label: Thesis
direcionamento.text: "A burn multiple you only see in board decks isn't a metric, it's a postmortem."

pautas.central_question: Why do founders with a great burn multiple still run out of cash?
structure: Define burn multiple in one sentence, no jargon
Explain the lag between when it's calculated and when it's acted on
Example: a team that hit target burn multiple by cutting the wrong spend
Show how to turn it into a monthly, forward-looking check instead of a quarterly grade
Close with the one question to ask before every hiring decision
pautas.keywords: burn multiple, startup metrics, fundraising, efficiency
pautas.tone: Practical. Turns a vanity metric into a working tool.

months.label: FEBRUARY / 2027
months.axis_title: THEMATIC AXIS: The Illusion of Growth Metrics
months.axis_description: Why the metrics that look best in a pitch deck are often the ones hiding the real problem.

pautas.title: "MRR growth can mask a dying business."

direcionamento.label: Common narrative
direcionamento.text: "MRR is up 20% month over month, we're winning"

direcionamento.label: Reality
direcionamento.text: Aggregate MRR growth can hide churn eating the base while a few large deals cover the gap

direcionamento.label: Angle
direcionamento.text: Founders who only watch the total number get blindsided when the large deals stop coming

direcionamento.label: Thesis
direcionamento.text: "Growing MRR and a healthy business are not the same claim. Only one of them survives a bad quarter."

pautas.central_question: Why do founders get blindsided by churn right after their best growth quarter?
structure: Show how blended MRR growth can hide segment-level decay
Explain the difference between net new and gross new revenue
Example: a company whose MRR chart looked perfect until one contract didn't renew
Give a simple cohort view founders can build without a data team
Close with what to report to the board instead of the single MRR line
pautas.keywords: MRR, churn, growth metrics, SaaS metrics
pautas.tone: Skeptical. Questions the metric everyone trusts by default.

pautas.title: "You don't have a growth problem. You have a definition problem."

direcionamento.label: Reality
direcionamento.text: Teams disagree internally on what 'growth' means (logos, revenue, usage) and optimize for different things without noticing

direcionamento.label: Angle
direcionamento.text: Most growth stalls are actually a coordination problem dressed up as a performance problem

direcionamento.label: Thesis
direcionamento.text: "Before you fix growth, agree on what you're growing. Half the time nobody actually agreed."

pautas.central_question: Why do sales, product, and the founder all think they're driving growth while the number stalls?
structure: Open with the scenario of three teams optimizing three different growth definitions
Explain why this misalignment is invisible until growth slows
Example: a team celebrating logo growth while revenue growth flatlined
Give a short exercise to force one shared definition across the team
Close with how to pick the one number that should drive decisions this quarter
pautas.keywords: growth strategy, alignment, startup metrics, prioritization
pautas.tone: Clarifying. Reframes a vague problem into a solvable one.

closing_sections.heading: Thematic Progression:
bullets: January → Cash as a decision tool
February → The illusion of growth metrics

closing_sections.heading: Connected Narrative:
paragraphs: Both months build toward the same idea: financial metrics are only useful when they change a decision before it's too late. Founders who treat numbers as a scoreboard react late; founders who treat them as a steering wheel act early.

closing_sections.heading: Target Audience:
paragraphs: Pre-seed to Series A founders managing their own finances without a dedicated CFO.

closing_sections.heading: Overall Tone:
bullets: Direct (names the gap between what founders say and do)
Practical (every piece ends in something usable this week)
Audience: Pre-seed to Series A founders
Language: Plain, no finance jargon without explanation
Objective: Position the newsletter as the place founders learn to use their numbers, not just read them
